name: Ganza
catalog_citation: Smolders, Joshua. 2016. A Phonology of Ganza (Gwàmì Nánà). Linguistic Discovery 14(1). DOI 10.1349/PS1.1537-0852.A.470. Dartmouth College (publisher HTML, full text).
catalog_locator: §6 Tone / §6.1 Tonemes; §3.3 Vowel Length; fn. 25; §7 Conclusion
catalog_quote: 6.1 Tonemes Ganza has two phonemic tones or tonemes, high (H) and low (L), both of which can occur as either associated or unassociated (floating) tones in the underlying form. A floating L will cause downstep (also called non-automatic downstep) of a following H, and is attested root-internally as well as between word and morpheme boundaries. ... Contour tones also exist, both falling and rising, but these are only ever realized on bimoraic syllables (i.e. double vowels or utterance-final lengthened vowels) and are best treated as two separate tonemes on adjacent TBUs. ... Tone carries a high lexical functional load in Ganza. It is a contrastive feature of noun and verb roots, as the tonal minimal pairs in (61) illustrate. ... [Conclusion:] I showed that Ganza has two tonemes— high (H) and low (L)— as well as phonemic downstep, and that these have a high functional load in the language…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all fragments of the deciding quotation (sec. 6.1 Tonemes, the functional-load sentence, sec. 7 Conclusion) and the domain quotation (sec. 3.3, fn. 27) are verbatim in the text we hold layer of the publisher HTML at the stated sections; fn. 25 (Hofmeister's 'accented syllable') is also there and is the only 'accent' token in the article; 'stress' never occurs. (2) The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule described' rests on a 2016 peer-reviewed, fieldwork-based, partly instrumental 59-page phonology article, which Glottolog and Crossref show to be the only published description of Ganza; no JIPA illustration, dissertation chapter on phonology, or handbook chapter exists that I could find (OHEL 2023 has no Ganza chapter; Smolders' later work is on Opo). (3) The only plausible upgrade is Melkamu Abate's AAU PhD (verb morphology, ELDP-funded), which is not in the AAU ETD

sources.note: Smolders fn. 25 reports Hofmeister called the H-toned negative-suffix syllable an 'accented syllable' (2010:19); seeing the passage would confirm this is an impressionistic label for H tone in Sudanese Ganza rather than evidence of a stress/accent system. Low stakes: Smolders already re-analyses it as tone.
